title: unsafe and pointers
sub: Pointers, native memory, Unsafe and MemoryMarshal
cards/0/body:
The unsafe keyword unlocks pointers: T*, taking an address with &, dereferencing with *, -> and arithmetic. The project has to allow it explicitly: <AllowUnsafeBlocks>true</AllowUnsafeBlocks>.

A pointer can only point to an unmanaged type: numbers, bool, char, enums, other pointers and structs made of them. You cannot take a pointer to a class or a string.

What goes away: bounds checks, type checks and — most importantly — the collector’s involvement. To the GC a pointer is just a number.
cards/0/deep: unsafe does not change the IL much: pointer arithmetic is plain add and ldind/stind. What changes is that the code becomes unverifiable: memory safety is now your guarantee. In .NET Framework this mattered for partial trust (CAS); .NET Core has no partial trust, and unsafe is just a compiler flag.
cards/1/title: The collector sees ref, not pointers
cards/1/body:
.NET has two kinds of "address":

  • A managed pointer — ref T, and what sits inside a Span<T>. The JIT tells the collector where such references live. If the object moves, the collector updates even a reference into its middle. No pinning needed.
  • An unmanaged pointer — T*, nint, IntPtr. The collector knows nothing about it. You may hold one to a heap object only while the object is pinned.

Hence the rule: for managed memory use ref and Span. Pointers are for memory the collector does not move: the stack, stackalloc, native memory, the POH.
cards/1/deep: A pointer to an unpinned heap object is the classic "GC hole". The code works thousands of times until a compacting collection lands exactly between taking the address and writing through it. Such bugs barely reproduce under a debugger. To hunt them the runtime has a debug mode, GC Stress, which triggers a collection at every point where one is possible. It is used mostly by the CLR developers themselves.
cards/2/q: You need a local "address" of the fifth element of a heap array and to write through it. What is safe without pinning?
cards/2/explain: ref int is a managed pointer: the collector knows about it and moves it along with the array during compaction. int*, IntPtr and nint are just numbers; once the array moves they point to nowhere.
cards/3/title: NativeMemory: memory the collector never sees
cards/3/body:
Since .NET 6 native memory comes from NativeMemory: Alloc, AllocZeroed, Realloc, Free, and the aligned AlignedAlloc and AlignedFree. It is a thin wrapper over the C library’s malloc/free.

What matters:

  • the collector does not see this memory: it is not part of the heap size, and the GC will not free it;
  • forget Free and you have a leak that only private bytes reveals (as in the "How to measure" unit);
  • free it in a finally, or via a SafeHandle if the memory lives as long as an object.
cards/3/deep: Before .NET 6 people used Marshal.AllocHGlobal: LocalAlloc on Windows, malloc on Unix. .NET 7 added NativeMemory.Clear, Copy and Fill. When memory runs out, Alloc throws OutOfMemoryException rather than returning null. The most convenient way to work with such memory is through Span<T>: it puts bounds checks on top of the raw pointer.
cards/4/q: Take a native buffer and make sure it is returned
cards/4/explain: Alloc allocates, Free returns the memory to the C library heap. Clear only zeroes the bytes, Realloc resizes, and NativeMemory has no Release method.
cards/5/title: Unsafe: unsafe without the unsafe keyword
cards/5/body:
The System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe class does what pointers do, but through ref — and needs no unsafe in your code. The collector sees the references, but types and bounds are on you.

  • Unsafe.As<T>(object) — treat a reference as a reference to T without a type check;
  • Unsafe.Add(ref x, n) — move a ref by n elements without a bounds check;
  • Unsafe.SizeOf<T>(), ReadUnaligned, SkipInit;
  • Unsafe.BitCast<TFrom, TTo> (.NET 8) — reinterpret the bits of a value.
cards/5/deep: Unsafe methods are JIT intrinsics: most compile to one or two instructions or vanish entirely. In the CoreLib sources many of them have a stub body with the IL in a comment, and the JIT substitutes the real implementation. The .NET libraries use them heavily in the inner loops of Span, strings and collections.
cards/6/body:
System.Runtime.InteropServices.MemoryMarshal lifts the restrictions on Span:

  • GetReference(span) and GetArrayDataReference(array) — a ref to the first element with no bounds check;
  • Cast<TFrom, TTo>(span) — see bytes as ints or structs without copying;
  • AsBytes, Read<T>, Write<T> — read and write structs in a byte buffer;
  • CreateSpan(ref x, length) — make a Span from a single ref.

The typical case is parsing a binary format right in the buffer, with no copies and no allocations.
cards/6/deep: Cast and Read work only with types without references — otherwise ArgumentException: turning bytes into a reference would mean forging an object address. Byte order is the machine’s (little-endian on x64 and ARM64); for portable formats use BinaryPrimitives.ReadInt32LittleEndian. Unaligned reads work on x64 and ARM64.
cards/7/q: Match the API with what it does
cards/7/pairs/0/1: A reference to another type, unchecked
cards/7/pairs/1/1: Moves a ref without a bounds check
cards/7/pairs/2/1: The same bytes as another type
cards/7/pairs/3/1: Memory the collector does not see
cards/7/pairs/4/1: A ref to the first array element
cards/8/body:
A bug in unsafe code rarely crashes right away. The typical story:

  • a write past the end of an array overwrites the header or type pointer of the neighbouring object;
  • the program keeps running — until the next collection;
  • during marking the collector follows the corrupted type pointer and crashes. The process dies with an internal CLR error, and the stack shows the GC, not your code.

So the rules are simple: unsafe code only in hot spots, after measuring; small isolated methods; tests at the boundaries; and Span with its checks wherever you can.
cards/8/deep: In a dump you hunt such corruption with the SOS command !verifyheap: it walks the heap and reports the first corrupted object. The neighbour right before it is the first suspect. Unsafe.As with the wrong type does the same more subtly: a virtual call through the "wrong" type pointer jumps through someone else’s method table.
cards/9/q: Which line holds the bug that makes the code write past the end of the array?
cards/9/explain: The condition i <= a.Length gives five iterations for four elements. Ordinary indexing would throw IndexOutOfRangeException, but Unsafe.Add silently writes the number into the memory after the array — most likely into the next object’s header.
cards/10/q: A loop was rewritten from a[i] to Unsafe.Add to remove bounds checks. The benchmark showed no difference. Why?
cards/10/options/0: The JIT already removes the bounds check in a loop from 0 to a.Length
cards/10/options/2: Bounds checks only run in Debug
cards/10/options/3: Adding to a long is slower than any check
cards/10/explain: The JIT proves that i is always within the array and emits no check (bounds check elimination). So a simple loop over an array or Span is already fast. Unsafe pays off where the JIT cannot prove it: strided walks, indices taken from another array.
cards/10/wrong/2: Bounds checks exist in Release too: they are part of memory safety, not a debugging feature.
cards/11/q: When is unsafe code justified? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: A hot loop where measurement showed that bounds checks cost noticeably
cards/11/options/1: A buffer for a native library that the collector must not see
cards/11/options/2: Parsing a binary protocol in a buffer without copying
cards/11/options/3: To speed up any code "just in case"
cards/11/explain: Unsafe code is a tool for bottlenecks and for talking to the native world. Without a measurement it only adds risk, and Unsafe.As in place of an honest cast turns a clear exception into memory corruption.
